content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
Summary
The authors propose solving data poison bi-level optimization using the meta learning formulation. 

Decision
Overall, I think the proposed meta-learning formulation seems legit, but I found the formulation of metalearning is hard to parse and the experimental comparison is not persuasive. Hence I recommend for weak reject.

Supporting argument:
1. The written can be improved in describing the meta learning formulation. Usually there is a clear definition of meta-learning training/testing tasks and training/test examples in each task. 
2. 16/255 is quite large for CIFAR10. What happen in other radius? Can the approach work in other constraints? 
3. In figure 4, the variance of the success rate, target loss are quite large. I wonder whether this means the approach is not stable.
4. Since it is the first clean-label poisoning attack on networks trained from scratch, it might be worth comparing the approach to other setup where there are some baselines.
5. The arrangement of figures are far away from text.
6. In Algorithm 1 Line 5, I don't get the part why there are M models instead of M-th model. In Lines 9, 10, the formulation is not clear. What's the reason for Line 11?
7. It is not clearly to me why there needs to be M models to consider. What's the performance with different M?


Additional feedback:
1. Footnote should go after period.

content.title: Thank you for the review
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their helpful comments. We understand the main concern that our writing is unclear and will work to improve it. Given the time involved to do so, we’ve decided to withdraw the paper for this review session. That said, below are our responses to the reviewer’s comments.

1. The written can be improved in describing the meta learning formulation. Usually there is a clear definition of meta-learning training/testing tasks and training/test examples in each task. 

The analogies to meta-learning can be laid out as follows:
Meta-variable: perturbations to the n poisons
Meta-train/meta-validation: training on poisoned minibatches for k SGD steps (meta-train), followed by evaluating the adversarial target loss (meta-validation)
Meta-test: fully training a classifier from-scratch for 50 epochs on the poisoned training set, followed by evaluating the adversarial target loss on that trained model

We will include a section on these analogies to meta-learning in the appendix.

2. 16/255 is quite large for CIFAR10. What happen in other radius? Can the approach work in other constraints? 

While our paper results are fixed to an epsilon of 16/255, lower values of epsilon also yield successes, at about a success rate of 30%. We will add an ablation experiment (currently running) where we look at the effect of epsilon on poisoning success.  Note that crafting a meta-poison is very computationally intensive, and so benchmarking methods and accurately quantifying success rates is time consuming.

3. In figure 4, the variance of the success rate, target loss are quite large. I wonder whether this means the approach is not stable.

Since there are many sources of stochasticity in training a network (initialization, minibatching, regularizers, batch norm, etc), the success of the poisoning attack is invariably stochastic as well, sometimes with high variance. We have found that one factor causing the large difference in the training curves in Figure 4 is changes to the base-target pair (which we randomize in Figure 4). For example, a poison-frog-target-plane is about 15% lower success on average than the poison-dog-target-bird pair. In our revision, we will separate the experiments by base-target pair and also add a distribution of success rates for each.

4. Since it is the first clean-label poisoning attack on networks trained from scratch, it might be worth comparing the approach to other setup where there are some baselines.

Since ours is the first data poisoning attack which works in the from-scratch training setting, we did not have other baselines to compare against. We will however, modify our method to work in the context of transfer learning (for which there are previous poisoning attacks), and compare our method to existing baselines for attacking transfer learning.

5. The arrangement of figures are far away from text.

We will fix this in the revision

6. In Algorithm 1 Line 5, I don't get the part why there are M models instead of M-th model. In Lines 9, 10, the formulation is not clear. What's the reason for Line 11?

We agree that setting an index for the M-th model would clarify this equation, as we are indeed computing Line 6 for all unroll steps 1, ..k  for each model M_i of the ensemble of M models. We have further clarified the writing in lines 9 and 10, where we use gradient computed in Line 8 to take a step toward minimizing the target loss (Line 9). In Line 10 we update all models by training for one epoch. This essentially draws new weights, i..e new tasks in a meta-learning perspective, for the poisons to be trained on. By the same reasoning, we reset a model in Line 11, if the maximum number of epochs is reached, so that we always draw weights from all phases of training and do not bias our weight draws towards networks later in training.

7. It is not clearly to me why there needs to be M models to consider. What's the performance with different M?

The need for an ensemble of M models is explained in Section 2.1: “To produce a transferable poison attack that is robust to changes in the initialization and training process, we average equation 2 over M surrogate loss functions, randomly initialized and independently trained.”  

We will add an ablation study in the appendix showing the dependence of the success rate on the number of models M.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper introduces a novel class of clean-label attacks of deep model training procedures (from scratch) using a meta-learning inspired approach. 

Pros:
1) Transferability across different training strategies is a particularly important novelty of this work, I think.
2) I find it particularly impressive that a clean-label attack is shown to work when training from scratch, which reduces the amount of knowledge about the model needed by the attacker.
3) The meta-learning formulation presented here may prove to be the starting point of many future investigations.
4) Multi-targeted attacks and third-party attacks appear to be novel contributions of this paper, but there is too little context given to judge that from the text alone.

Cons:
1) The figures are not too informative. Could you please provide more examples in an appendix?
2) The writing could be much improved, especially for making the paper more accessible to a wider audience.
3) Details of the meta-learning procedure and related works are almost non-existent. While the authors provide a discussion of what's possible and challenging for current adversarial attack methods, many details and citations are missing. This makes the many comments and explanations in the text obscure, although they may be correct and insightful. Could you please work on the writing and assume that I know nothing of the SOTA in adversarial attacks? I am willing to read the paper again.
4) There is far too little detail about experimental procedures. Please provide a detailed discussion with references to established procedure or previous works!
- What are the meta-training/meta-validation and meta-testing sets? 
- What is a reasonable baseline you could compare against? If nothing else, please argue for that in the paper and perhaps provide an ablation of your method as a baseline.

As far as I can tell, the paper may be introducing an approach with potential, but many clarifications are required. The paper is not self-contained enough to even attempt to guess how important or novel the presented results are. Hence, all I can do is judge the little I have managed to understand from the paper. While this may be enough for a workshop, I cannot at this point recommend acceptance, primarily because of the writing.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
In this paper, the authors propose a new model to generate adversarial poisoning examples. The generation model is based on MAML and the experiments partially show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The problem is interesting and using MAML to generate adversarial poisoning examples is timely. However, my concerns are:

1. The paper is not well-organized. For example, (1) the first section should be named as "Introduction"; (2) In figure 6, the location of three figures is not in a line.
2. The technical contribution is limited. The authors simply apply MAML to generate adversarial poisoning examples. The motivation is clear but the design is quite straightforward. No new attack/defense models are proposed. I think the contribution is lower than the acceptance bar of ICLR.
3. No baselines are compared. The authors should compare the proposed model with other adversarial sample generation methods in the experiments.

content.title: Thank you for the review
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their helpful comments. We understand the main concern that our writing is unclear and will work to improve it. Given the time involved to do so, we’ve decided to withdraw the paper for this review session. That said, below are our responses to the reviewer’s comments.

1. The paper is not well-organized. For example, (1) the first section should be named as "Introduction"; (2) In figure 6, the location of three figures is not in a line.

We will work to better organize the layout and figure positioning of our paper

2. The technical contribution is limited. The authors simply apply MAML to generate adversarial poisoning examples. The motivation is clear but the design is quite straightforward. No new attack/defense models are proposed. I think the contribution is lower than the acceptance bar of ICLR.

We are *not* using MAML to craft poisoning examples. MAML and meta-learning terminology are invoked in our work in order to provide a common vocabulary to describe the rather complicated process of crafting and evaluating poisons (terms like meta-gradients, meta-crafting, meta-testing are useful to distinguish them from their “non-meta” counterparts).

At its most basic level, we use a bi-level optimization strategy to craft poisons. MAML is also based on bi-level optimization, but MAML is not unique in applying bi-level methods to machine learning. For example, bi-level optimization methods similar to MAML have also been applied in a popular differentiable neural architecture search (DARTS, Liu et al. 2018).

The novel aspects or contributions of our work are as follows:
Our bi-level formulation backprops to the poison inputs, rather than the architectural hyperparameters (as in DARTS) or the weight initialization (as in MAML)
Our method deals with a more complex solution space. For example MAML must find an initialization that results in a good validation accuracy after 1 SGD step of 5 examples. In contrast, MetaPoison must find a (norm-bounded) input perturbation resulting in low adversarial loss after 50 epochs of training on random mini-batches sampled from 50000 examples, starting from any random weight initialization.
Our method handles the randomness in _when_ the poisons appear with minibatches. For each forward pass, only a few or none of the poisons will be present in that minibatch. Further, the metagradients for each poison must be averaged across the M models before being applied, which is made difficult since the poisons show up at different times in each model (each model samples minibatches independently and randomly). We introduce a per-epoch metagradient update strategy to deal with this complexity. See Algorithm 1.
We present a unique and effective method to simplify the inner optimization of training the network on the current set of poisons. Unrolling the entire training pipeline of 50 epochs on a single computation graph would be prohibitively space intensive. Instead we take a small number of SGD steps **initialized at uniformly sampled points along the training trajectory of the base network**. This ensures that the poisons aren’t designed to induce low adversarial error only in the beginning of training but throughout the training process.
Importantly, our method achieves high poisoning success rates on from-scratch training with a realistic, well-established architecture (Resnet18) and dataset (CIFAR10).

3. No baselines are compared. The authors should compare the proposed model with other adversarial sample generation methods in the experiments.

Ours is the first data poisoning attack that targets from-scratch training, and we did not have other baselines to compare against. We will however, slightly modify our method to work in the context of transfer learning (for which there are previous poisoning attacks), and use that to compare our method against existing baselines.
